citation: Bussière, Chinn, Ferrara, Heipertz (2022), The New Fama Puzzle, IMF Economic Review 70(3); NBER WP 24342
main_claim: The forward-premium puzzle in eight USD pairs holds before the financial crisis but reverses afterwards (Fama coefficient large and positive)
mechanism: Change in co-movement of expectation errors and interest differentials; survey expectations support UIP more consistently
supporting_evidence: Eight USD exchange rates; survey expectations
methodology: Fama-coefficient analysis (method named only implicitly in the abstract)
limitations: Abstract only; sample period not stated on the page
sample_period: not stated on the page read (pre- vs post-crisis split)
testability: Testable on single pairs; regime split around 2008
data_needed: Daily rates and rate differentials (have: FRED H.10, DTB3, JGB)
publication_vs_sample: Post-crisis reversal documented before our validation window; our validation lies in the authors' 'new puzzle' period

citation: Brunnermeier, Nagel, Pedersen (2008), Carry Trades and Currency Crashes, NBER Macroeconomics Annual 23; NBER WP 14473
main_claim: Carry-currency moves are negatively skewed because carry trades unwind suddenly when risk appetite and funding liquidity fall
supporting_evidence: Table 3: a higher rate differential predicts higher excess returns for 5-6 quarters and strongly negative future skewness (coefficient about -24, s.e. about 4, quarters t+1 to t+7); cross-section of average skewness vs average differential R2 81%; JPY has the most negative differential and the highest positive skewness (funding currency); VIX and TED increases coincide with carry losses and position unwinds; high VIX/TED levels predict higher future carry returns
methodology: Panel regressions with country fixed effects (quarterly; Newey-West, 10 lags) of excess FX returns, CFTC non-commercial futures positions and realised within-quarter skewness on the interest differential; predictors of skewness and risk reversals (Table 4); weekly regressions on VIX and TED changes; VAR impulse responses
limitations: In-sample only; 8 currencies, 1986-2006 (one regime of positive JPY carry); futures positions are a partial proxy (most carry trading is OTC forwards); peso-problem caveat for realised skewness (authors); long-run under/overreaction 'cannot make a definite statement' (authors); the October 1998 USD/JPY crash link to carry unwinding is a conjecture; no trading-rule or cost evaluation
sample_period: daily rates aggregated to quarterly 1986-2006; weekly 1992-2006; risk reversals 1998-2006; AUD, CAD, JPY, NZD, NOK, CHF, GBP, EUR vs USD (Datastream 3-month interbank rates)
testability: Would be weakened by: no negative skewness for USD/JPY carry after 2006 in independent data; VIX/TED level not predicting carry returns out of sample. For us: describes crash risk of being long USD/JPY when the differential is wide; not a validated timing rule (our V139/V140 risk-off filters were killed)

citation: Engel, Kazakova, Wang, Xiang (2022), A Reconsideration of the Failure of Uncovered Interest Parity for the U.S. Dollar, Journal of International Economics; NBER WP 28420
main_claim: Interest differentials are a fragile, unstable predictor of USD excess returns and lose all power near the zero lower bound; y.o.y. inflation differentials do predict excess returns from the mid-1980s
mechanism: Markets underreact initially to predictable future monetary-policy changes (authors' interpretation)
supporting_evidence: Interest-differential slope: negative before 2007, positive after (JPY: -2.45 in 1987-2006, +3.61 in 2007-2020); medium-run JPY slope -40.1 (1987-2006) vs +29.1 (2007-2020, p 0.018). Inflation-differential panel slope -0.091 (p<0.01, 1987-2020). Output gap and growth rarely significant
contradicting_evidence: For JPY itself the inflation-differential slope is insignificant in every sample (full -0.125 p 0.24; 1987-2020 -0.016 p 0.89; 1987-2006 -0.213 p 0.28; 2007-2020 +0.187 p 0.20); authors cannot rule out a risk premium; West (2012): instability may mean returns are unpredictable; FX006
methodology: Monthly Fama (1984) regressions of USD excess returns on interest differentials (1-month LIBOR) and on y.o.y. inflation differentials, with Amihud-Hurvich (2004) small-sample bias corrections; 10-year rolling windows; medium-run (12-month rolled) and long-run (VAR-based) versions; fixed-effects panels with Driscoll-Kraay errors; subsamples 1979:06/1987:01-2020:09, 1987-2006, 2007-2020
limitations: In-sample regressions only, no out-of-sample forecast or trading evaluation; 'findings here are not definitive' (authors); JPY is the main exception in the panel; monthly frequency; no costs
sample_period: 1979:06-2020:09 monthly (JPY full span); DataStream to 2017-11, FRED after; G10 vs USD
testability: Would be invalidated by: the inflation-differential slope failing out of sample after 2020, or turning positive across currencies as JPY did. For USD/JPY specifically the paper gives NO support for an inflation-differential rule; the interest-differential relation reversed sign around 2007, consistent with our killed carry trials (V135/V136)
data_needed: CPI inflation for US/Japan/UK (ALFRED vintages for point-in-time US CPI; Japanese/UK vintages not yet sourced)
our_result: rate-differential trials killed; inflation-differential idea untested and not supported for JPY by the paper itself
publication_vs_sample: Published 2021/2022 inside our validation window; any test on 2015-2023 overlaps the authors' sample

citation: Lustig, Roussanov, Verdelhan (2011), Common Risk Factors in Currency Markets, Review of Financial Studies 24(11); NBER WP 14082
main_claim: A global 'slope' risk factor explains most of the cross-sectional variation in high- vs low-rate currency portfolio returns
mechanism: High-rate currencies load more on a global risk factor; carry is compensation for global risk, especially in bad times
methodology: Portfolio sorts on interest rates; factor model
limitations: Abstract only; return figures and sample not on the page; cross-sectional (many currencies), not single-pair
sample_period: not stated on the page read
testability: Not directly testable on one pair; motivates the single-pair caveat
our_result: single-pair carry killed (consistent with the caveat)

citation: Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling, Schrimpf (2012), Carry Trades and Global Foreign Exchange Volatility, Journal of Finance 67(2)
main_claim: High-rate currencies lose when global FX volatility rises unexpectedly; a volatility-risk proxy captures more than 90% of the cross-section of five carry portfolios
mechanism: Volatility risk premium; low-rate currencies hedge volatility shocks
supporting_evidence: Carry portfolio H/L earns more than 5% p.a. net of bid-ask; the volatility factor explains more than 90% of the cross-section of the five portfolios; liquidity factors lose significance when volatility is included; also prices FX momentum, US equity and corporate-bond cross-sections
contradicting_evidence: FX002 (funding-liquidity crash view); the authors 'cannot rule out' volatility being a summary measure of liquidity
methodology: Monthly cross-sectional asset pricing: currencies sorted into 5 forward-discount portfolios each month (48 currencies; 15 developed subsample), net of bid-ask spreads; global FX volatility = average absolute daily return across currencies, innovations from a full-sample AR(1); GMM/Fama-MacBeth pricing; liquidity factors (TED, bid-ask, Pastor-Stambaugh) as alternatives
limitations: Volatility innovations estimated on the full sample, 'preventing pure out-of-sample tests' (authors); cross-sectional, many-currency result, not a single-pair timing rule; developed-country subsample shows a less monotonic pattern; sample ends Aug 2009
sample_period: Nov 1983-Aug 2009 monthly (BBI/Reuters spot and 1-month forwards via Datastream); options 1996-2009
testability: Would be invalidated by: the volatility-beta relation failing in post-2009 cross-sections. For USD/JPY alone it says the yen (a funding currency) tends to gain when global FX volatility rises unexpectedly; it is a risk description, not a forecast

citation: Chen, Tsang (2013), What Does the Yield Curve Tell Us About Exchange Rate Predictability?, Review of Economics and Statistics 95(1) 185-205, DOI 10.1162/REST_a_00231 (version read: author version June 2011)
main_claim: Relative Nelson-Siegel factors predict exchange-rate changes and excess currency returns 1-24 months ahead: a 1 pp rise in a country's relative slope or level factor is followed by ~3-4% annualised appreciation of its currency; a relatively steeper curve precedes depreciation
mechanism: Yield curves embed expectations of output and inflation; risk premia respond to them (asset-pricing view)
supporting_evidence: Monthly Aug 1985-Jul 2005 for CAD, GBP, JPY vs USD; corroboration 1991-May 2011; SPF survey correlations
contradicting_evidence: FX003; own rolling out-of-sample forecasts do not consistently beat a random walk or a single-maturity differential
methodology: Monthly regressions on relative Nelson-Siegel factors; small-sample inference corrections; rolling OOS (online appendix)
limitations: In-sample evidence; OOS weak by the authors' account; curvature least robust
data_needed: Zero-coupon or par yields US/Japan/UK (have US H.15, JGB MoF; UK not yet)
our_result: killed (V142 validation Sharpe 0.47 but in-sample -0.26; neighbour V141 negative)
publication_vs_sample: Sample ends 2005/2011; our in-sample 1991-2014 overlaps it; our validation 2015-2023 is after publication

citation: Neely, Weller, Ulrich (2009 journal; read: St. Louis Fed WP 2006-046B, rev. March 2007), The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis: Evidence from the Foreign Exchange Market
main_claim: FX technical-rule excess returns of the 1970s-80s were genuine, but filter and moving-average profits had disappeared by the early 1990s; less-studied rules declined but probably not completely
mechanism: Adaptive markets: learning and competition erode profitable rules
supporting_evidence: True out-of-sample tests of previously studied rules
contradicting_evidence: FX008 (cross-sectional momentum persists with limits to arbitrage)
limitations: Abstract and introduction only; high volatility limits precision
sample_period: 1970s onward (end date not on the pages read)
testability: Explains why no FX price-trend trial was pre-registered
publication_vs_sample: Decline documented after publication of the early studies (the point of the paper)

citation: Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling, Schrimpf (2012), Currency Momentum Strategies, Journal of Financial Economics 106(3)
main_claim: Cross-sectional currency momentum shows a winner-minus-loser spread of up to 10% p.a. that is hard to exploit because of very effective limits to arbitrage
mechanism: Under- and over-reaction; limits to arbitrage
supporting_evidence: Not explained by traditional risk factors; partly by transaction costs; distinct from carry

main_claim: Diversifying the carry trade across currencies boosts the typical Sharpe ratio by over 50% for a currency trader

citation: Ranaldo, Söderlind (2007 WP; 2010 journal), Safe Haven Currencies, SNB Working Paper 2007-17
main_claim: Franc, euro, yen and pound tend to appreciate against the USD when US stocks fall, US bond prices rise and FX volatility rises, over hours to several days
supporting_evidence: Daily JPY/USD: significant on S&P (t 2.84) and FX volatility (t 3.13); CHF strongest safe haven, GBP weakest; 1998: yen up about 9% (31 Aug-7 Sep) and 12% (7-8 Oct), attributed by BIS and commentary partly to carry unwinding
contradicting_evidence: JPY/USD Treasury-note coefficient insignificant (t 0.54); JPY/EUR appreciates when the S&P strengthens (mixed safe haven); effects partly reverse the next day
methodology: OLS regressions (Newey-West) of currency depreciation on contemporaneous and one-period-lagged S&P futures returns, 10-year Treasury-note futures returns and a principal-component FX volatility measure, at 3-, 6-, 12-hour and 1-, 2-, 4-day horizons; kernel partial-linear models for non-linearity; cross-rates; event studies (1998 Russia, 9/11, 2004 Madrid)
limitations: Mostly contemporaneous co-movement, not prediction; 'further lags were not significant'; daily R2 for JPY/USD 0.02; Reuters FXFX indicative quotes; 1993-2006 only; signs in tables lost in our text extraction
sample_period: 1993-2006, 5-minute Reuters FXFX mid quotes (Olsen for GBP), CME/CBOT futures
testability: Would be invalidated by: no yen appreciation against the USD on large equity sell-offs or volatility spikes after 2006. For us it supports describing the yen as a partial risk-off currency at the same moment, not a tradable lead
data_needed: VIX, S&P, US bond prices (have VIX)

citation: Ito (2002), Is Foreign Exchange Intervention Effective?: The Japanese Experiences in the 1990s, NBER WP 8914
main_claim: Japanese interventions April 1991-March 2001 earned ~9 trillion yen, sold yen only below 125 and bought only above 125, were effective in the late 1990s; joint US-Japan operations were 20-50 times more effective
mechanism: Leaning against deviations from a long-run mean; coordination amplifies effect
supporting_evidence: Newly disclosed official data; profit calculations
methodology: Regressions of daily yen/dollar changes on intervention; profit accounting
limitations: Abstract only; disclosure date not on the page; data not observable in real time during the sample
testability: Descriptive event study only (intervention was secret in real time)
our_result: no trial (excluded with reason in the pre-registration)
publication_vs_sample: Record disclosed after the sample; any 'rule' would use future information

citation: Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold, Vega (2003), Micro Effects of Macro Announcements, American Economic Review 93(1); NBER WP 8959
main_claim: Announcement surprises cause jumps in exchange rates; responses depend on timing and the sign of the surprise; bad news has a greater impact than good news
supporting_evidence: Conditional-mean adjustment is a jump within the first 5-minute interval, little movement after; Yen/$ contemporaneous return response per 1 s.d. surprise: payroll 0.072%, trade balance 0.115%, durable goods 0.029%, initial claims -0.009% (all significant at 5%); good US growth news appreciates the dollar
contradicting_evidence: Sign asymmetry varies by indicator and currency (absent for Pound/$ and Euro/$ on payroll)
methodology: 5-minute returns regressed on own lags and lags of standardized announcement surprises (41 US and German indicators; MMS median survey as expectation), weighted least squares with a volatility model; news impact curves for sign asymmetry
limitations: Expansionary 1990s only (authors: data cover only good times); needs licensed consensus forecasts, which we do not have; Reuters indicative quotes; FOMC timing approximations before 1995; no trading evaluation
sample_period: 3 Jan 1992-30 Dec 1998, 5-minute Olsen/Reuters quotes, 1,724 days after filtering; MMS surveys
testability: Would be invalidated by: no first-interval jump at scheduled releases in independently time-stamped data. For us it supports the 0-5 s payroll timestamp test and event windows; it gives no edge without consensus data
data_needed: Intraday FX (BLOCKED pending cross-vendor check) and licensed consensus forecasts (not available)
publication_vs_sample: Pattern documented long before any test we could run

citation: Chaboud, Chernenko, Wright (2007), Trading Activity and Exchange Rates in High-Frequency EBS Data, Federal Reserve IFDP 903 (related JEEA 2008)
main_claim: After US announcements volume spikes even when data match expectations; at one-second frequency the price jumps immediately with little volume, then volume and volatility surge about 15 seconds later; UK holidays sharply reduce volume
mechanism: Information arrival and liquidity provision dynamics
